what_it_does: High-level synthesis (HLS) is a process that translates software code into a hardware circuit blueprint (a chip design) automatically. A modern style of HLS called 'dynamically scheduled dataflow' produces circuits where each piece of computation fires as soon as its inputs are ready, without a global clock pulse telling it when to go — like an assembly line where each station starts the moment parts arrive. Sharing a resource (for example, one memory bank accessed by multiple parts of the circuit) while keeping everything pipelined is difficult without a central controller, which limits which software programs can be turned into efficient hardware. PipeLink restructures the synthesis process into two phases — a compile phase and a link phase (borrowing the idea from software building) — so that shared functions and shared memory can be accessed in a fully pipelined, asynchronous way. This is said to support a broader class of general software programs than previous approaches, though the specific benchmarks and numbers are in the full paper.
